video.title: 4 Tips For Consistently Crushing Slow Balls

classification.reason: The coach teaches four core technical and visual principles for attacking and crushing slow balls consistently, using player demonstrations and drills.

problem.title_as_question: How do you consistently attack and crush slow balls?
problem.definition: Slow, floating balls lack incoming court penetration and pace, making them deceptively difficult to attack without proper forward balance, hand preparation height, early contact, and precise visual tracking.
prerequisites: ability to recognize a short floater

symptoms.description: Player remains stationary or finishes with weight on the back foot instead of stepping forward through contact.
The hitting hand drops excessively below the incoming floater before forward swing.
Attacking drives on slow balls result in erratic errors or forced moonballs.
Swing feels disconnected from the ball in space, hitting through an approximate point in the air.

causes.statement: The slow ball drops straight down without court penetration, requiring the player's body and back foot to proactively drive forward into positive balance.
Preparing the hitting hand way below the slow ball makes driving flat impossible and forces an inconsistent spin stroke or a moonball.
Failing to react early and sprint up allows the floater to drop below net height, eliminating the margin to drive the ball flat.
The brain does not view the slow ball as threatening, leading the player to look away and lose exact visual tracking of the bounce in space.

angles.summary: Because a slow ball lacks forward penetration, the player must achieve positive balance where the back foot lands in front of its starting point.
The coach has the demonstrator hit while staying stationary to show how unnatural and ineffective slow ball attacks become without forward weight drive.
Preparing the hand level with the ball creates a nearly flat diagonal drive rather than an exaggerated low-to-high loop.
Players think slow balls are harmless and do not require close tracking, causing them to swing at random spots in space.

solutions.summary: Wrap an elastic resistance band around the waist and press forward against the resistance while self-drop-feeding slow balls to train forward leg drive.
solutions.external_goal: Press forward against the resistance of the elastic band toward the court.

solutions.summary: Look at the ball's incoming height and prepare the hitting hand at that exact height to drive through it flatter.
solutions.external_goal: Align the hand with the height of the incoming ball.

solutions.summary: Recognize the floater early and sprint forward to make contact while the ball is still above net height.
solutions.external_goal: Contact the ball two to three feet above the top of the net.

solutions.summary: Keep eyes locked on the ball all the way to watching it physically hit the court ground before striking.
solutions.external_goal: Watch the ball hit the court surface.
